title: Database Cost: Reserved Instances, Aurora Options & Serverless
summary: Reserved DB instances, Aurora I/O-Optimized vs Standard, Serverless v2 and cheaper dev databases.
tldr: Steady 24/7 databases → **Reserved DB instances** (RDS, Aurora), **reserved nodes** (ElastiCache, Redshift, OpenSearch). Compute Savings Plans do **not** cover managed databases.

Aurora storage choice: **Aurora Standard** pays per I/O (cheap when I/O is low); **Aurora I/O-Optimized** has no I/O charges but higher instance and storage prices (cheaper when I/O is a large share of the bill). Choose per cluster.
Idle or spiky databases → **Aurora Serverless v2** (scales in fine-grained ACUs; minimum 0 ACU auto-pauses). Dev/test → stop on a schedule, use **Aurora clones** instead of full restores.
Backups: keep **automated backups / PITR** for the short window and an **AWS Backup** rule for long monthly retention, instead of keeping every daily or hourly snapshot.

keyFacts.text: AWS guidance: when I/O charges exceed about a quarter of Aurora cost, I/O-Optimized is usually cheaper. Low-I/O clusters should stay on Standard.
Aurora Serverless v2 can scale to zero and pause when idle, then resume on the first connection after a short delay. Billed per ACU-hour.
A stopped RDS or Aurora DB restarts automatically after seven days, so dev databases need a recurring stop schedule, not a one-time stop.
Aurora clones share storage pages with the source and only pay for pages that change, so daily QA copies of a large database are cheap and fast.
Database Savings Plans (Dec 2025): 1-year spend commitment across Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB and more. Flexible but shallower discount than 3-year reserved instances.

traps: Compute Savings Plans don't apply to RDS, Aurora or ElastiCache; databases use reserved instances/nodes or Database Savings Plans.
Buy reservations **after** moving to the target instance class (for example Graviton r7g); reserving the old class doesn't transfer across families.
Setting automated backup retention to years is impossible (maximum 35 days); long retention needs AWS Backup or manual snapshots.
Stopping an RDS instance once isn't enough; it restarts after 7 days.
Aurora Backtrack rewinds the cluster in place; it doesn't replace PITR or long-term backups.
